title: US Tech Layoffs Cross 100,000 in 2026 as Europe's Most Valuable Company Offers €20,000 Bonuses to Retain Staff
excerpt: While American tech workers face a second consecutive year of mass job cuts driven by AI restructuring, Dutch chipmaker ASML is paying employees to stay through 2030.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US tech layoffs surpassed 100,000 in the first half of 2026, exceeding 2025's total.
  • India accounts for 7.16% of global AI-led tech layoffs from 2020 to 2026.
  • ASML offers €20,000 bonuses to retain employees through 2030 amid industry layoffs.
  • Major companies like Dell and Meta have cut thousands of jobs due to AI restructuring.

  • Tech layoffs in the US have exceeded 100,000 in the first half of 2026, already surpassing the full-year 2025 total
  • India ranks second globally in AI-led tech layoffs, accounting for 7.16% of all cuts between 2020 and 2026
  • ASML, Europe's most valuable company, is offering all eligible employees a €20,000 retention bonus to stay through 2027-2030
  • Major companies including Dell (11,000 jobs), Meta, Google, IBM, Atlassian, and Intuit have all cut thousands of positions citing AI transformation

The US tech industry's layoff crisis has deepened in 2026, with cumulative job cuts exceeding 100,000 in the first six months alone — already outpacing the entirety of 2025. The surge comes as companies across Silicon Valley restructure their workforces around artificial intelligence, eliminating roles they say are being made redundant by automation while simultaneously hiring for AI-specific positions.

The Scale of Cuts

The list of companies shedding workers reads like a who's who of American tech. Dell eliminated roughly 11,000 positions — about 10% of its workforce — spending $569 million on severance alone. Meta cut around 10% of its Reality Labs division. IBM has shed an estimated 15,000 US roles since late 2024, with Bloomberg reporting the company plans to triple entry-level hiring for AI and hybrid-cloud positions even as it lets go of existing staff.

Atlassian cut 1,600 jobs (10% of staff), with CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes offering a notably candid assessment: "Our approach is not 'AI replaces people.' But it would be disingenuous to pretend AI doesn't change the mix of skills we need." Intuit eliminated 3,000 roles (17% of its workforce), Snap cut 1,000 positions, and Google has quietly reduced headcount across its Cloud division through rolling performance reviews and voluntary buyouts.

India Second Worst Hit

India has emerged as the second most affected country globally, accounting for 7.16% of all AI-led tech layoffs between January 2020 and July 2026, according to NDTV's analysis of industry data. The US leads with 71.33%, followed by Germany at 3.43% and the UK at 2.64%. For Indian IT professionals — both in India and those on H-1B visas in the US — the dual pressure of domestic layoffs and tightening immigration policies has created an acutely stressful environment.

"It would be disingenuous to pretend AI doesn't change the mix of skills we need or the number of roles required in certain areas. It does."

— Mike Cannon-Brookes, CEO, Atlassian

ASML Bucks the Trend

Against this backdrop of austerity, ASML — Europe's most valuable company by market capitalisation and the sole maker of the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines essential for cutting-edge chip production — is going in the opposite direction. The Dutch firm confirmed plans to offer all eligible employees a conditional stock grant worth approximately €20,000 ($22,838) if they remain with the company between 2027 and 2030.

ASML, which employs 44,500 workers globally including around 8,500 in the US, reported net income of €2.92 billion in its latest quarter. Its flagship lithography tools are nearly sold out through 2027. The retention bonus follows similar moves by Samsung Electronics, TSMC, and SK Hynix — all paying premiums to keep skilled semiconductor workers as chip demand surges.

What It Means for Indian Tech Workers

The divergence between software layoffs and hardware retention highlights a structural shift in the global tech labour market. For Indian engineers and IT professionals, the message is increasingly clear: skills in AI, semiconductors, and hardware engineering command a premium, while traditional software development and middle management roles face compression. The semiconductor industry's willingness to pay for retention contrasts sharply with the software sector's willingness to cut.
